extra.explain: Assignment binds a name to a value; it does not link the two names. `y = x` copies the reference at that instant, so rebinding `x` afterwards leaves `y` where it was.
The right-hand side is evaluated fully before anything is assigned, so `a, b = b, a` builds the tuple `(2, 1)` from the old values and only then unpacks it. No temporary variable needed.
`//` divides and rounds towards negative infinity, giving an int when both sides are ints.
The surprise: `//` floors rather than truncating, so it rounds DOWN, away from zero for negatives. -3.5 floors to -4, not -3. This bites in binary search and midpoint arithmetic.
`/` is true division and ALWAYS produces a float, even when the result is a whole number. Use `//` when you want an int, especially for indices.
`%` is the remainder left after floor division.
Python's `%` always takes the sign of the RIGHT operand, so -7 % 3 is 2, not -1 as in C or Java. Useful for wrapping an index: `i % n` is always in range.
`divmod(a, b)` returns the floor division and the remainder together as a tuple, doing in one step what `a // b` and `a % b` do in two.
`int(s)` parses a string of digits into a number. Python never converts implicitly, so `\"42\" + 1` is an error rather than 43.
Zero, the empty string and the empty list are all falsy, so `if not xs:` is the idiomatic empty check. Careful: it cannot tell an empty list from a zero.
Strings index like lists, and indexing gives a one-character string. Python has no separate char type.
Negative indices count from the end: -1 is the last character, -2 the second last. Shorter and safer than `len(s) - 1`.
`s[a:b]` takes from a up to but NOT including b, so the length of the slice is exactly b - a. The half-open convention is why `s[:i] + s[i:]` reassembles the original.
A slice takes `[start:stop:step]`, and a step of -1 walks backwards, so `s[::-1]` is the whole string reversed.
Strings cannot be changed in place. Every string method returns a NEW string and leaves the original alone, so ignoring the return value does nothing.
`sep.join(parts)` is called on the separator, not on the list. Building a string by repeated `+=` in a loop is quadratic; join is linear.
`ord` gives a character's code point and `chr` reverses it. `ord(c) - ord('a')` maps 'a'..'z' onto 0..25, which is how you index a 26-slot count array.
`b = a` does not copy the list, it gives the same list a second name, so mutating through either is visible from both. This is the single most common source of surprise bugs in Python.
`a[:]` builds a new list with the same elements, so appending to the copy leaves the original alone. Note it is a SHALLOW copy: nested lists inside are still shared.
`[[0] * 2] * 2` repeats the same inner list object twice, so both rows are the same list and writing to one writes to both. Almost never what you want for a grid.
The comprehension evaluates `[0] * 2` afresh each iteration, producing genuinely separate rows. This is the correct way to build a 2-D grid.
`list.sort()` sorts in place and returns None, while `sorted(xs)` leaves the input alone and returns a new list. Writing `xs = xs.sort()` silently sets xs to None.
`key` takes a function applied to each element to decide the ordering; the elements themselves are returned unchanged. `key=len` sorts by length.
`range(n)` counts 0, 1, ... n-1 — n values, ending one before n. The exclusive end is why `range(len(xs))` covers exactly the valid indices.
With a negative step the range counts down, and the end is still exclusive, so `range(3, 0, -1)` stops at 1 and never reaches 0.

extra.explain: Iterating a dict yields its KEYS, not its values or pairs. Since Python 3.7 they come back in insertion order.
The conditional expression reads value-if-true, condition, value-if-false. It is an expression, so it can sit anywhere a value can.
Comparisons chain the way they do in mathematics: `1 < 2 < 3` means `1 < 2 and 2 < 3`, and the middle value is only evaluated once.
`or` returns one of its OPERANDS, not True or False: the first truthy one, else the last. Hence `x or default` as a fallback.
`and` returns the first falsy operand, else the last. It also short-circuits, so the right side is never evaluated when the left is falsy — which is what makes `i < len(xs) and xs[i]` safe.
`is` compares identity, `==` compares value. For None always use `is`, since a class can define `==` to do anything.
`d.get(k, default)` returns the default when the key is missing instead of raising KeyError, so it needs no `in` check first.
`d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1` is the standard counting idiom: read with a default of 0, add one, store back. `collections.Counter` does the same thing.
`d.setdefault(k, [])` returns the existing value, or inserts the default and returns THAT, so the append lands in the dict. `defaultdict(list)` is the tidier version.
A set stores each value once and tests membership in constant time, which is why converting to a set is the usual way to de-duplicate or to check 'have I seen this'.
Unpacking assigns positionally, so the number of names must match the number of values.
A comprehension builds a new list by evaluating the expression for each element.

extra.explain: The default is evaluated ONCE, when the function is defined, so a mutable default is shared by every call and accumulates. Use `None` as the default and build the list inside instead.
`all([])` is True and `any([])` is False, which follows from `all` meaning 'no counterexample'. Worth knowing before relying on either for an empty input.
AND keeps a bit only where BOTH numbers have it. 5 is 101 and 3 is 011, so only the last bit survives: 001, which is 1. `x & 1` is the standard odd/even test.
OR sets a bit where EITHER number has it. 101 | 011 = 111, which is 7. Used to switch flags on.
XOR sets a bit where the two DIFFER. 101 ^ 011 = 110, which is 6.

Anything XORed with itself is 0, and anything XORed with 0 is unchanged. XOR is also order-independent, so XORing a whole list cancels every value that appears twice and leaves the one that appears once — the entire trick behind Single Number.
`~x` flips every bit, which in two's complement equals -x - 1. Python integers are conceptually infinite-width, so the sign bit extends forever and the result is negative rather than wrapping.
Shifting left by n multiplies by 2**n, filling with zeros. `1 << n` builds a mask with only bit n set.
Shifting right by n divides by 2**n and discards the bits shifted off. `x >> 1` is a halving step.
Right shift on a negative number keeps the sign and rounds DOWN, matching `//` rather than truncating towards zero. -5 // 2 is -3, not -2.
To read bit n, shift it down to the bottom and mask with 1. 13 is 1101, so bit 2 is 1.
`n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit: 12 is 1100 and 11 is 1011, leaving 1000. Repeating it counts set bits in as many steps as there are ones, rather than 32.
`n & -n` isolates the lowest set bit, because -n is ~n + 1, which flips everything above that bit and leaves it alone. 12 is 1100, so the answer is 100.
`bin` renders an int in binary with an '0b' prefix; slice with [2:] to drop it. `bin(x).count('1')` counts set bits in one line.
